transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-09
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~54 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Lina (CTO), Samir (ML Eng), Priya (Security), Ben (Product)

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE walked Hydra through an onramp migration roadmap from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to the Redwood API. Main agenda: parity mapping for completions/chat/function-calling, demo of Redwood Console and Optimize suggestions (batching, caching, quant profiles), security and private deployment options (VPC/KMS), and POC plan + benchmarks. Customer is primarily concerned with 1) preserving prompt/response parity (temperature/stop-sequences/formatting), 2) latency and cost tradeoffs at 10M tokens/day scale, and 3) SOC2/KMS + VPC control for sensitive data.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everybody, thanks for joining, um i'll do a 2 minute intro then hand off to jonas for the parity mapping demo. lina, thanks for putting the team together.
[00:14] Lina: thanks, maya. quick note, we have about 50 minutes, and then priya has another meeting so we'll try to get her questions earlier.
[00:22] Jonas: great, i'll share screen, uh just a sec - i'm on the Redwood Console, home dashboard. so overview first: our goal today is to show how your current OpenAI + Anthropic flows map to Redwood API calls, what changes are minimal, and where Optimize suggests cost/latency wins.
[00:35] Ben: can you call out the big breaking differences? like sampling, streaming, function calls — is there a huge refactor?
[00:41] Jonas: short answer no. long answer: there are surface changes. model names are different, function call schema is similar, streaming works same. the biggest work is around tokenization differences and stopping logic, and also prompt prefixing we saw in some Anthropic flows.
[00:58] Samir: when you say tokenization differences, do you mean the byte pair stuff? how do we ensure the few-shot prompts give same length + costs?
[01:08] Jonas: yeah so models differ, the tokenizers can shift counts by a few percent. our parity sheet — which i'll send — has a mapping of model families and observed token delta vs the equivalent OpenAI/Anthropic model. for example, together-1.1 style vs redwood-v2-medium shows ~+4% tokens on average for long prompts. you can mitigate by prefix trimming, or switching to a medium quant profile which impacts latency slightly but reduces cost.
[01:30] Priya: important for us is security - encryption and retention, KMS keys and audit logs. how does Redwood handle customer-managed keys and VPC?
[01:40] Maya: good question. for Private deployments we support VPC peering and bring-your-own KMS via our enterprise package. hosted API can be configured with encrypted-at-rest and optional HSM integration; we provide audit logs and SIEM hooks. i'll attach SOC2 + KMS integration notes.
[01:56] Priya: ok please send that. also we need an answer on data residency - do you have EU regions?
[02:02] Maya: yes EU regions available, and Dedicated pools can be isolated per-customer. we'll include region options in the sheet.
[02:10] Jonas: back to parity - i want to demo a live mapping. i'm pasting a sample Anthropic chat and then a Redwood API equivalent.
[02:20] [Screen share noise / typing sounds]
[02:28] Jonas: here's the Anthropic prompt, they were using assistant-style system messages with length-limited context and a custom stop sequence. in Redwood, we recommend sending the system as a structured instruction (we support both raw system messages and structured tool calls). the stop sequence maps to Redwood's stop_token parameter; sometimes we need to translate special sequences, that is explained line-by-line in the parity sheet.
[02:50] Samir: function calling - we have heavy usage for structured extraction, will our current functions map 1:1?
[02:56] Jonas: yes 90% maps 1:1. minor things: the argument serialization and enums had subtle differences; Redwood's SDK includes a thin shim in our client that normalizes enum casing and numeric types. for complex nested objects we've seen some customers need a couple of unit tests to validate parity.
[03:18] Lina: how about streaming? our product uses streaming to show partial answers, do you preserve chunking / partial tokens?
[03:25] Jonas: streaming is supported with two modes: standard SSE and binary frames for low-latency clients. chunk boundaries may differ slightly due to batching at the runtime, but in practice customers saw identical UX. if you need token-level parity for e.g. real-time UI we can route to low-latency pools which reduce batching windows.
[03:44] Ben: costs - what's the typical token cost delta? we aggregate ~10M tokens/day across completions and embeddings.
[03:51] Maya: cost varies by model and quantization. Optimize will run a predictive simulation: for your workload we expect 10-20% reduction with prefix/KV caching + a medium quant profile vs running same model unquantized on competitor endpoints. dedicated pricing can give bigger per-token cost reductions. we'll provide an example calc in the parity sheet.
[04:13] Samir: can you explain KV cache — our app uses long conversations that reuse context heavily.
[04:18] Jonas: KV cache stores the transformer key/value states so when you append messages you don't recompute earlier layers; for session-heavy workloads this can be 2-3x throughput improvement and large cost savings. Redwood supports prefix caching and sticky session routing for that. note: some vendor SDKs don't have sticky session support by default which causes cache misses — we call that out in the migration guide.
[04:41] [05:00] Jonas: demo: Console -> Optimize tab. here you can see suggested batching windows, recommended quant profiles per endpoint, and per-route latency vs cost curves. the UI also shows which model variants are compatible fallbacks if capacity constrains the primary.
[05:16] Ben: what about rollouts and A/B?
[05:19] Jonas: Console has a rollout engine: you can route X% to redwood-v2-medium and Y% to a fallback smaller variant; automatic fallback-to-hosted or to dedicated pool is supported. we also expose traces at the token level for diffs.
[05:34] Priya: tracings sound great, do they include PII masking?
[05:38] Jonas: we can mask by default and redact tokens depending on your retention policy. those settings are per-route and per-token-class.
[05:46] Lina: timelines — if we wanted to move off OpenAI/Together in production, what is a realistic POC -> prod timeline?
[05:53] Maya: typical is 2 weeks for on-recorded POC (hosted), then a 4–6 week integration for pilot with private endpoints and SSO if needed. Dedicated/private deployments add provisioning time (2—4 weeks) depending on region and change controls.
[06:08] Samir: we have a lot of existing prompts and eval harnesses. do you integrate with Eval frameworks for continuous quality checks?
[06:14] Jonas: yes — Redwood Optimize can run evals against a prompt set; we also have an API for automated regression detection and alerting. we'll ingest your existing evals or you can use our JSON schema.
[06:26] Ben: any gotchas when porting embedding use-cases (we use openai embeddings for vector DB)?
[06:31] Jonas: embeddings are straightforward but watch for vector-dim differences and normalization. Redwood includes a mapping table to ensure your nearest-neighbor thresholds stay stable; sometimes reindexing is needed but it's usually a small effort.
[06:44] [06:58] Priya: legal/procurement — our procurement wants contract language around data deletion and return of customer data post-termination. do you support that?
[07:05] Maya: yes we include data deletion clauses; for Private deployments you're in control of retention, for Hosted we support deletion workflows and can provide a certificate.
[07:13] Lina: okay if we're comfortable on security and cost, i want to see a benchmark run that mirrors our peak load.
[07:19] Maya: that's part of the POC plan. jonas will set up a 10M tokens/day workload with same prompt mix.
[07:24] Jonas: i'll need Samir's sample dataset and a sample traffic profile. after this call i'll share the benchmark script and invite a run.
[07:31] Samir: i'll share the dataset by end of day.
[07:34] Jonas: perfect. quick note on model variants: if you're coming from Anthropic's claude-style flows we recommend redwood-claude-compat, but we've tuned redwood-v2 to be the default for most customers; it'll likely need small prompt tweaks for safety filters.
[07:51] Ben: about safety filters — we've seen content moderation differences causing false positives on some customer content. can we tune the safety?
[07:58] Jonas: safety filters are configurable. you can choose to run inline checks, or run a lightweight moderation endpoint pre-filtering. we keep audit logs of decisions for appeals.
[08:09] [08:30] Lina: demo the API call sample please, show a before (OpenAI) and after (Redwood).
[08:36] Jonas: sure. here's an OpenAI-style call: completion with temperature:0.7, top_p:0.9, stop:["\n"], and then their chat messages. here's Redwood equivalent — same fields mostly, parameter names map 1:1 in our SDK, temperature and top_p preserved, and we add an optional 'pin_model_version' flag to freeze the checkpoint.
[08:57] Samir: pin_model_version — is that per-route or per-request?
[09:01] Jonas: it's per-route default but can be overridden per-request. useful during rollouts to avoid drift.
[09:07] Priya: downtime / reliability — what are your SLOs for hosted API?
[09:12] Maya: hosted API SLA is 99.9% for enterprise customers with dedicated pools offering stricter guarantees. we also provide regional fallback routing to avoid single-region outages.
[09:23] Ben: curious about model updates — if a public model gets updated, do you force changes on our side?
[09:29] Jonas: customers control model versions and rollouts; we don't auto-migrate. we'll notify and provide compatibility notes.
[09:36] Lina: fine. any reference customers in financial services or healthcare?
[09:40] Maya: yes we have several health and fintech customers on dedicated pools; i'll share a redacted case study.
[09:47] [10:00] Ben: how do we measure latency vs cost tradeoff in Optimize? show the graph.
[10:05] Jonas: Optimize simulates your request mix and produces a curve; you can pick operating points. it also suggests batching window sizes that respect your p99 latency SLO. for example, if you target p99 < 300ms we'll recommend smaller batch windows with KV cache.
[10:22] Samir: do we need to change client-side retry logic?
[10:26] Jonas: basic retry semantics are the same but we recommend idempotency keys for high throughput and to avoid duplicate completions. we also expose a request id to tie logs to traces.
[10:35] Priya: about SSO and RBAC — we need SCIM + SAML and fine-grained role control for dev/prod separation.
[10:42] Maya: supported; we also have token-scoped keys and route-level permissions. for highly regulated setups we can map your internal roles to console roles via SCIM.
[10:52] Lina: okay we're coming up on time. let's summarize next steps.
[10:57] Maya: recap — 1) we'll send parity spreadsheet + pricing + SOC2/KMS docs; 2) ops will provision a 2-week hosted POC with trial credits; 3) jonas will prepare benchmark script; 4) schedule the benchmark and decide pilot timeline.
[11:12] Ben: sounds good. priya — any outstanding blockers?
[11:16] Priya: just the security pack and KMS confirmation, plus procurement questions about contract terms.
[11:23] Maya: we'll get that over in the pack.
[11:26] Samir: i'll share dataset tonight.
[11:29] Lina: thanks everyone. maya, jonas, please include the parity mapping examples for our most used prompts and the embedding dimension notes.
[11:36] Jonas: will do.
[11:38] Maya: thanks all. meeting end.
